entries.title: Khmer at a glance
body: Khmer is the official language of Cambodia, with about 17 million speakers. It is an Austroasiatic language, related to Mon and Vietnamese rather than to Thai or Lao, though centuries of contact mean they share many words.
Unlike its neighbours, Khmer is not tonal. It has a large set of vowel sounds and many two-consonant clusters at the start of words. Words never change form.

examples.t: ខ្ញុំ{កំពុង}រៀនភាសាខ្មែរ

entries.title: How Khmer script works
body: Khmer script has 33 consonant letters and is written without spaces between words. Each consonant belongs to one of two series, and the series changes how the vowel after it is said: the same vowel mark gives aa after a first-series consonant and ea after a second-series one.
When two consonants meet with no vowel between them, the second is written below the first as a subscript (ជើង, “foot”), as in ខ្ញុំ (khnhom).

entries.title: Numbers and Khmer digits
entries.body: Six to nine are built on five: ប្រាំមួយ (5 + 1) is six. Khmer digits are used everywhere, alongside 0–9.

entries.title: The sampeah
entries.body: The sampeah (សំពះ) is the Cambodian greeting: palms pressed together with a slight bow. The higher the hands, the more respect, from chest height for friends to the forehead for monks and the king. Cambodian New Year, Choul Chnam Thmey, falls in mid-April.
